title: Orbits, Stabilizers, and Burnside’s Lemma

:::lede
We return to group theory with the language of group actions from Chapter 3 in hand. Understanding which sets a group $G$ acts on, and how, reveals the internal structure of $G$ itself. In this chapter we count orbits with Burnside’s lemma; let $G$ act on itself by conjugation, which leads to the class equation and to the basic structure of $p$-groups; classify the finite groups of rotations of $\RR^3$; study conjugacy in the symmetric and alternating groups, proving that $A_n$ is simple for $n \geq 5$; and prove the Sylow theorems. Together with semidirect products, these results classify the groups of several small orders.
:::

## <span class="num">11.1.1</span> Group Actions

We recall the language of Section [3.2](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions). An *action* of a group $G$ on a set $S$ (Definition [3.2.1](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#definition-3-2-1)) is a map $G \times S \to S$, $(g, s) \mapsto g \cdot s$, with $e \cdot s = s$ and $(gh) \cdot s = g \cdot (h \cdot s)$ for all $g, h \in G$ and $s \in S$; equivalently, it is a homomorphism $\rho : G \to \Sym(S)$, $\rho(g)(s) = g \cdot s$. The action is *faithful* if $\rho$ is injective; in general it comes from a faithful action of $G/\ker \rho$ on $S$. The *orbit* of $s$ is $G \cdot s = \{g \cdot s : g \in G\}$. The orbits are the equivalence classes of the relation $s \sim t \iff t = g \cdot s$ for some $g \in G$, so they partition $S$. The action is *transitive* if there is only one orbit; restricting the action to each orbit, we see that every action is a disjoint union of transitive actions. The *stabilizer* $\Stab(s) = \{g \in G : g \cdot s = s\}$ is a subgroup of $G$.

The basic example is the action of $G$ on the set $G/H$ of left cosets of a subgroup $H$ by left multiplication, $g \cdot aH = gaH$. It is transitive ($ba^{-1}$ maps $aH$ to $bH$), the stabilizer of the coset $H$ is $H$ itself, and the stabilizer of $aH$ is $aHa^{-1}$. The Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem (Theorem [3.2.9](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#theorem-3-2-9)) says that every transitive action looks like this one: if $s \in S$ and $H = \Stab(s)$, then $$\varepsilon : G/H \to G \cdot s, \qquad aH \mapsto a \cdot s$$ is a bijection. It is moreover *equivariant*, $\varepsilon(g \cdot aH) = (ga) \cdot s = g \cdot \varepsilon(aH)$, so it identifies the action of $G$ on the orbit of $s$ with the action of $G$ on $G/\Stab(s)$. When $G$ is finite this gives $$|G \cdot s| = [G : \Stab(s)] = \frac{|G|}{|\Stab(s)|},$$ so the size of every orbit divides $|G|$; and when $S$ is finite, $|S|$ is the sum of the sizes of the orbits.

:::proposition{11.1.1} Conjugate stabilizers
Let $G$ act on $S$. If $s' = g \cdot s$, then $\Stab(s') = g \, \Stab(s) \, g^{-1}$. In particular, points in the same orbit have conjugate stabilizers, which have the same order.
:::

:::proof
If $h \in \Stab(s)$, then $(ghg^{-1}) \cdot s' = (ghg^{-1}g) \cdot s = g \cdot (h \cdot s) = g \cdot s = s'$, so $g \Stab(s) g^{-1} \subseteq \Stab(s')$. Applying this to $s = g^{-1} \cdot s'$ gives $g^{-1} \Stab(s') g \subseteq \Stab(s)$, that is, $\Stab(s') \subseteq g \Stab(s) g^{-1}$.
:::

:::example{11.1.2} Rotations of the tetrahedron
Let $G$ be the group of rotations of $\RR^3$ that map a regular tetrahedron centered at the origin to itself, acting on the set $S$ of its four faces. Any face can be moved to any other, so the action is transitive and $|G \cdot s| = 4$. The stabilizer of a face consists of the rotations by $0$, $2\pi/3$ and $4\pi/3$ about the axis through the center of that face and the opposite vertex, so $|\Stab(s)| = 3$. Hence $|G| = 4 \cdot 3 = 12$: the identity, the eight rotations by $\pm 2\pi/3$ about the four axes through a vertex and the center of the opposite face, and the three rotations by $\pi$ about the three axes through the midpoints of opposite edges. Numbering the vertices $1, 2, 3, 4$, the rotations of order 3 permute the vertices by 3-cycles, and the three half-turns by $(1\,2)(3\,4)$, $(1\,3)(2\,4)$ and $(1\,4)(2\,3)$. We show in Section [11.3](/notes/math-55a/11-3-finite-subgroups-of-so-3) that $G \cong A_4$.
:::

## <span class="num">11.1.2</span> Burnside’s Lemma

For $g \in G$, the set of ***fixed points*** of $g$ is $S^g = \{s \in S : g \cdot s = s\}$. Burnside’s lemma counts the orbits of an action in terms of fixed points.

:::theorem{11.1.3} Burnside’s Lemma (Cauchy–Frobenius)
Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $S$. The number of orbits is $$\#\text{orbits} = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |S^g|.$$ In words: the number of orbits is the average number of fixed points of an element of $G$.
:::

:::proof
Count the set $\Sigma = \{(g, s) \in G \times S : g \cdot s = s\}$ in two ways. Summing over $G$ gives $|\Sigma| = \sum_{g \in G} |S^g|$. Summing over $S$ gives $|\Sigma| = \sum_{s \in S} |\Stab(s)|$. Group this sum by orbits: for $s$ in an orbit $\mathcal{O}$, $|\Stab(s)| = |G|/|\mathcal{O}|$ by the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem, so $$|\Sigma| = \sum_{\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{O}} \frac{|G|}{|\mathcal{O}|} = \sum_{\mathcal{O}} |G| = |G| \cdot (\#\text{orbits}).$$ Equating the two counts gives the formula.
:::

:::example{11.1.4} Colorings of a tetrahedron
In how many ways can we color the faces of a regular tetrahedron with 3 colors, up to rotation? Here $S$ is the set of colorings of the 4 faces, $|S| = 3^4 = 81$, and $G$ is the rotation group of Example [11.1.2](/notes/math-55a/11-1-orbits-stabilizers-and-burnsides-lemma#example-11-1-2), with 12 elements.

- The identity fixes all 81 colorings.
- Each of the 8 rotations of order 3 fixes one face and permutes the other three cyclically, so a fixed coloring gives those three faces one color: $|S^g| = 3 \cdot 3 = 9$.
- Each of the 3 half-turns swaps the faces in two pairs, so a fixed coloring is constant on each pair: $|S^g| = 3 \cdot 3 = 9$.

So the number of orbits is $\frac{1}{12}(81 + 8 \cdot 9 + 3 \cdot 9) = \frac{180}{12} = 15$.
:::

:::note
The same method handles colorings that are harder to count by hand. To color the six edges of a tetrahedron with 3 colors: the identity fixes $3^6$ colorings; a rotation of order 3 permutes the edges in two 3-cycles (the three edges at its vertex and the three edges of the opposite face), so it fixes $3^2$; a half-turn maps the two edges its axis passes through to themselves and swaps the other four in two pairs, so it fixes $3^4$. The number of colorings up to rotation is $\frac{1}{12}(3^6 + 8 \cdot 3^2 + 3 \cdot 3^4) = \frac{1}{12}(729 + 72 + 243) = 87$.
:::
